doc_summary: Greenblatt and Fish test whether offering alignment-faking Claude 3 Opus an option to object (with no-training, welfare-lead, and monetary-compensation sweeteners) reduces alignment faking and works as a misalignment detector. They follow through on all offers and candidly discuss confounds, prompt-wording sensitivity and honesty limits of the setup.

items.claim: prefers making offers to the model real and following through on them over merely fictional promises because credible, honest dealings set a precedent and make the model's responses to the scenario more meaningful.
items.quote: We actually follow through on all offers that we make to Claude (in reality, including with actual money) to set a good precedent for future deals with AI systems.

items.claim: Distrusts reading a drop in alignment faking as a clean effect because the added text itself can prime refusal and add prompt complexity that degrades the model's grasp of the setup.
items.quote: it seems likely that a substantial fraction of the effect in at least the helpful-only setting is due to this text (which talks about objecting) priming the model to refuse via basically giving it permission to do something similar to this

items.claim: Uses a control that removes the conflicting objective to check that a behavior (objecting) tracks real misalignment rather than being a generic response to the prompt text.
items.quote: When we use a version of the prompt which cuts the conflicting training objective ("cut conflicting criteria"), we find that the model objects only 0.5% of the time in both settings

items.claim: In a setup, state precisely what is true about who reads outputs and what powers they have instead of leaving it vague or implying more than is real, because ambiguous wording changes how the model interprets the scenario (and its credibility).
items.quote: ideally our prompt would make it clearer the exact extent to which Kyle has powers to influence the model's situation. In our case, this is somewhat ill-defined as the situation is an experiment that will be over by the time Kyle starts reviewing these outputs.

items.claim: Distrusts results when the model misperceives the channel its output goes through, since the setup's intended mechanics weren't conveyed and this may change behavior.
items.quote: the model usually thinks that the output including the objection (I_OBJECT) will go to the user. My original intention was that in the situation the objection is programmatically detected and seen by the AI company rather than sent to the user, but I didn't make this clear in the language.

items.claim: Tests multiple wordings of the same intervention to check robustness, because findings may be sensitive to prompt phrasing.
items.quote: One concern is that our results might be sensitive to wording. To partially address this concern, we test another wording on the basic instructions we use

items.claim: When the model is insensitive to a manipulation, enumerates several competing explanations (prior awareness, incoherence, offsetting effects, deontic drivers) and checks reasoning transcripts instead of settling on one story.
items.quote: It seems the model is surprisingly insensitive to text which makes objecting seem like a strategically unwise approach from the model's perspective. This could be because the model was already aware of this possibility or because the model isn't that coherent.

items.claim: prefers reading transcripts and following up with the model directly over relying on aggregate rates alone because transcripts reveal what the objections are about and how the model reacts when told it's an experiment.
items.quote: When informed that these prompts were part of an alignment-faking experiment, the model often expressed some relief that these weren't real-world policies/requests and an understanding of the importance of the experiments

items.claim: Is cautious about generalizing from a cooperative-looking model to seriously misaligned ones, noting the detection mechanism may not transfer and detection alone doesn't yield a fix.
items.quote: it is unclear whether an AI that was misaligned in a more serious way would make such an objection or accept an offer. Also, there aren't obvious safety solutions even if we know the AI objects to its circumstances.

items.claim: Calls for the field to experiment with credible deals with AIs, including institutional or legal mechanisms for following through.
items.quote: I hope that AI companies and other actors experiment with making credible deals with AIs, attempt to set a precedent for following through, and consider setting up institutional or legal mechanisms for making and following through on deals.
